title: Blood on My Hands
subtitle: 12 records. No fame. The most dangerous bass music ever made.

slides.text:
Sam Shackleton.
Lancashire born. Punk bands at 16.
Then he heard dubstep at FWD>>.

Everything changed.
slides.image_concept: London night alley, distant club entrance with light leaking out, fog
slides.image_keywords: london night alley club door light fog

slides.text:
2003. He starts producing.
Not from a studio background.
Not from money.

From percussion.
From sub-bass.
From dub.
slides.image_concept: Dark studio with analog synthesizers and sampler, tangled cables
slides.image_keywords: analog synthesizer dark studio cables vintage

slides.text:
2005. Skull Disco is born.
With Appleblim. Bristol.

African drums. Middle Eastern scales.
Sub-bass that moves the floor
before the drop exists.

This was not dance music.
This was ritual.
slides.image_concept: Collage of African percussion and subwoofer speaker in dark room
slides.image_keywords: african percussion tribal drums dark room

slides.text:
12 releases. 3 years.

No mainstream press.
No radio play.
No celebrity DJ co-sign.

The music moved city by city
through the people who needed it.
slides.image_concept: 12 vinyl records in a record case, handwritten labels
slides.image_keywords: vinyl record collection rare underground handwritten label

slides.text:
"Blood on My Hands." 2007.

17 minutes.
No chorus.
No drop.

Just percussion spiraling inward
and bass that never resolves.

Critics called it avant-garde.
The dancefloor called it home.
slides.image_concept: Dark dancefloor with crowd silhouettes, single overhead light
slides.image_keywords: dark dancefloor silhouette crowd club underground

slides.text:
2008. Skull Disco closes.

2010. Woe to the Septic Heart! opens.
His own label. Deeper. Stranger.

The sound gets longer.
More meditative.
Less genre. More world.
slides.image_concept: Blank white vinyl record label with handwritten text, minimal
slides.image_keywords: blank vinyl record label white minimal handwriting

slides.text:
The most honest music
does not ask to be understood.

It asks to be felt.

Save this.

slides.image_keywords: silhouette speaker light dark room minimal
